newsitem.title: INDIA: India 97/98 budget can be approved -- United Front.
newsitem.headline: India 97/98 budget can be approved -- United Front.

text.p: A new centre-left United Front government would be able to get parliamentary approval for the 1997/98 budget, a senior coalition official said on Friday.
"If there is a regular new government, the same budget with necessary amendments will go through," said the United Front official, who asked not to be identified.
A United Front spokesman said earlier on Friday that the defeated alliance expects to form a new centre-left government by April 21 with the support of the Congress party.
"The formation of a new government is entirely likely before parliament resumes on the 21st (of April)," coalition spokesman Jaipal Reddy told reporters in the Indian capital.
Congress triggered Deve Gowda's downfall in a vote of confidence last week after it withdrew its support for his 10-month-old government.
President Shankar Dayal Sharma has agreed to help move the budget in a special session of parliament from April 21 to 23.
Technically, the 1997/98 (April-March) budget, handed down by Finance Minister P. Chidambaram in February, is leftover legislation from Deve Gowda's government.
The budget has been hailed by industry for its plans to cut corporate taxes, lower income tax and reduce import tariffs.
Last week, finance ministry officials said the Appropriation Bill and the Finance Bill would be placed before parliament for approval.

The Appropriation Bill, already examined by a parliamentary panel, lists the demands for grants or spending proposals by various ministries. The Finance Bill gives effect to the tax and tariff proposals outlined in the 1997/98 budget.
"The Finance bill is now a property of the house," the United Front official said.
The government so far has been empowered by a vote-on-account, or a bill authorising spending for 1996/97 programmes, until mid-May.
If the Finance Bill is not passed by then, the old tax and tariff rates set by Deve Gowda's government in its 1996/97 budget would continue to hold.

The Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Friday suggested the extension of the budgetary proposals beyond mid-May by an ordinance to avert any constitutional crisis in view of the political impasse, the Press Trust of India (PTI) reported.
Both BJP and the Congress have indicated that they will push for some amendments in the Finance Bill, the news agency said.
